design_detail: Observational dose-response study inside a single 30-day inpatient admission on a research unit, with no non-using comparison group. Fifty-six people who used cocaine, all with cocaine metabolites in urine on admission, were tested with a neuropsychological battery 1 to 3 days after admission and again on day 28 or 29, with abstinence enforced and checked by random urine screens. Participants had been recruited into two categories, cocaine (fewer than 10 drinks a week, n = 29) and cocaine plus alcohol (more than 10 drinks a week over at least 2 years, n = 27), but the analysis does not compare the groups: because drug-use histories overlapped, all 56 were pooled and analysed by hierarchical multiple regression, entering age, sex and estimated IQ first, then alcohol (drinks per week) and its square, then cocaine (grams per week) and its square, both exposures log-transformed. Session 2 was analysed by analysis of partial variance, entering the session 1 score for the same test first, then the alcohol and cocaine terms, then interactions of dose with the admission score. Exposure was self-reported past use, recalled at admission; cocaine grams per week were derived from reported weekly spending at an assumed price and purity.
can_establish: That among 56 people who used cocaine, mostly by smoking, higher self-reported weekly cocaine use and higher self-reported weekly drinking were each associated with worse scores on particular tests 1 to 3 days after admission, after adjustment for age, sex and estimated IQ, and that for three measures a further dose-related change appeared by 4 weeks of enforced abstinence.
cannot_establish: That cocaine or alcohol caused any of these differences (observational, exposure recalled, no pre-use measurement); that the scores represent impairment (no non-using comparison group and no normative comparison are reported); that the two drugs act additively (no cocaine-by-alcohol interaction term is reported at session 1); that the effects persist (persistence is inferred from the absence of a significant change at session 2, with practice effects uncontrolled); or anything about people who drink without using cocaine, since every participant used cocaine.

sample.recruitment: Recruited by a research corporation through newspaper advertisements; admitted to a clinical inpatient research unit of a national drug-abuse research programme for 30 days, given no treatment or medication during the stay, and paid for their time (pp. 2285–2286).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cocaine as drug of choice; use by any route for at least 2 years; use at least four times a month; urine positive for cocaine metabolites on admission, taken as showing use in the previous 24 to 48 hours. The cocaine group reported fewer than 10 drinks a week; the cocaine plus alcohol group more than 10 a week over 2 years. Excluded for current or past DSM-III-R dependence on any psychoactive substance other than cocaine, including alcohol; for urine positive for substances other than cocaine and its metabolites; for current or past psychiatric disorder; and for neurological illness, head trauma with loss of consciousness, seizure disorder, stroke, abnormal neurological examination or pregnancy. Caffeine or tobacco dependence was allowed, and the authors note it was impractical to limit their use despite their vascular effects (p. 2286).
sample.demographics: Mean age 34.34 (SD 4.55) in the cocaine group and 33.93 (5.46) in the cocaine plus alcohol group; 79% and 81% men; 86% and 85% African American; education 12.03 (1.66) and 12.15 (1.06) years; Shipley estimated IQ 93.97 (8.22) and 97.56 (10.15); WAIS-R Vocabulary 37.00 (11.94) and 38.74 (12.76); SCL-90-R depression 56.07 (9.77) and 55.07 (14.59). Smoking was the main route for all participants and 84% (47 of 56) used cocaine only by smoking (Table 1 and Results, p. 2287).
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported between the two sessions, but the degrees of freedom in the analyses range from 46 to 54 against a sample of 56, which is not explained (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited people who named cocaine as their drug of choice, who were medically and psychiatrically screened, and who were willing to stay on a research unit for 30 days without treatment. The sample is predominantly African American men who smoked cocaine, which the authors state limits generalization. Because dependence on any other substance, including alcohol, was an exclusion, the heavier-drinking group consists of people drinking above 10 drinks a week who did not meet criteria for alcohol dependence, a narrower exposure than the group label suggests. Everyone used cocaine, so there is no cocaine-free and no drug-free comparison.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at admission through a structured interview, the Drug Use Survey Questionnaire, the Addiction Severity Index and the Diagnostic Interview Schedule: days used in the last 14 and 30 days, years used, age at first use and duration of longest use. Weekly cocaine in grams was not measured directly but derived from reported weekly spending, converted at an assumed 100 US dollars per gram at 50% purity, a price taken from a drug-enforcement estimate for the city. Alcohol was recorded as days per week and number of drinks per week, a drink being a glass of wine, a shot or 12 ounces of beer; where the two instruments disagreed, their average was used. Urine toxicology confirmed recent cocaine use at admission and random screens during the stay confirmed abstinence (pp. 2286, 2291).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: cocaine 2.80 (SD 4.37) g a week in the cocaine group and 2.18 (2.08) in the cocaine plus alcohol group, on 4.20 (1.67) and 4.38 (1.20) days a week, for 7.07 (4.97) and 8.91 (5.59) years; alcohol 3.73 (4.84) and 17.51 (23.18) drinks a week on 0.86 (0.81) and 3.23 (1.05) days a week, for 14.90 (8.27) and 15.19 (7.45) years. Route: 84% smoked cocaine exclusively (Table 1 and Results, p. 2287).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on substances other than cocaine was excluded and admission urine had to be negative for other substances, so other illicit drug use is largely designed out but not quantified. Tobacco and caffeine use was permitted and is not reported at all, although the authors name their vascular effects as a reason it would have been preferable to limit them. Alcohol is the second exposure of interest and is modelled, not excluded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Session 1 at 1 to 3 days after admission, with cocaine metabolites in urine on admission showing use within the previous 24 to 48 hours; session 2 on day 28 or 29 of an enforced-abstinence stay, with random urine screens throughout. All testing was in the morning (p. 2286).

comparison.controls: None. There is no non-using comparison group and no alcohol-only group; every participant used cocaine, and the comparison is between people with more and less self-reported use within this sample. The session 2 analysis uses each person's own session 1 score as the comparison.
comparison.matching: Not applicable; age, sex and Shipley estimated IQ were entered as covariates. Education, tobacco, caffeine, route and years of use were not adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement of any kind. Premorbid ability is represented only by the Shipley estimate taken after years of use, which the authors use as a proxy; the correlations they cite against reverse causation (Shipley IQ with cocaine grams per week r = 0.164, with drinks per week r = 0.226) have 95% intervals of about -0.10 to 0.41 and -0.04 to 0.46 (editors' calculation, Fisher z, n = 56), so they do not exclude a moderate association.

outcomes.instruments: Shipley Institute of Living Scale (estimated IQ) and WAIS-R Vocabulary; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (total, learning rate as trial 5 minus trial 1, delayed recall, recognition errors); WAIS-R Digit Symbol, Trails A, Trails B and Stroop Color-Word for executive function; WAIS-R Block Design for visuoperception and visuoconstruction; the California Computerized Assessment Package for simple and choice reaction time, including a go/no-go task (false positives, number correct) and a repetition-of-numbers task; Grooved Pegboard for manual dexterity; SCL-90-R for depressive symptoms. Administered by a trained psychometrician supervised by a neuropsychologist (p. 2286).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments with published norms, but no normative comparison is reported: scores are analysed only as continuous outcomes within this sample. The Shipley estimate is reported to correlate 0.79 with WAIS-R full-scale IQ.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Decrement' is operationalized as a statistically significant regression coefficient for a drug-dose term, in either linear or squared form, after covariates; the paper reports no cut-off, no comparison with norms and no clinical criterion for impairment. Persistence is operationalized as the absence of a significant further dose effect at session 2 after adjustment for the session 1 score.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 18 test scores were available from the battery; Tables 2 and 3 report only those with significant drug terms, and each outcome was tested against four drug terms (alcohol, alcohol squared, cocaine, cocaine squared) at session 1 and against further dose-by-admission-score interactions at session 2, all at P < 0.05. The authors name the use of multiple, possibly correlated dependent variables as their first limitation (pp. 2286, 2290).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The examiner was blind to the intensity and duration of drug use (p. 2286). Groups were not formally compared, so group assignment could not unblind the testing.

analysis.effect_sizes: F statistics with degrees of freedom, P thresholds and the proportion of variance accounted for by the full model (R-squared total 0.20 to 0.50 at session 1 and 0.53 to 0.68 at session 2, the latter including the admission score). No regression coefficients, no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes are printed, and the models' R-squared cannot be separated into the part due to the drug terms. Editors' calculation of partial correlation-squared from each printed F and its degrees of freedom gives 0.08 to 0.24 for the session 1 drug terms (for example go/no-go number correct F(1,47) = 14.63, partial r-squared 0.24; RAVLT total F(1,48) = 7.01, 0.13; Trails B alcohol-squared F(1,48) = 8.23, 0.15), so each single drug term accounts for roughly 8 to 24% of the residual variance in the test it predicts.
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and Shipley estimated IQ, entered first in every model; the alcohol terms were entered before the cocaine terms, so cocaine effects are reported over and above alcohol. Education, tobacco and caffeine use, route, years of use, days per week and depressive symptoms were not adjusted for. Both exposures were log(x+1) transformed.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified primary outcome; the authors state the hypothesis that the heaviest use would go with the poorest performance, based on their own earlier work.
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 2 and 3 list only the variables with significant dose effects (9 of the battery at session 1, 3 at session 2); results for the remaining tests, including Trails A, simple and choice reaction time and the recognition and delayed-recall measures at session 1, are not reported. Session 1 and session 2 group means and standard deviations for any test are never shown, in either the tables or the figures.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 56 participants and up to 7 predictors, and with the two exposures nearly uncorrelated (r = -0.13, 95% interval about -0.38 to 0.14, editors' calculation), the design has reasonable power only for moderate dose effects; absent effects on tests not listed in Tables 2 and 3 cannot be read as showing no association.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within a sample of 56 people who all used cocaine, higher self-reported weekly drinking was associated with worse scores on executive and motor tests (Trails B, Stroop, Digit Symbol, Block Design, Grooved Pegboard), mostly in a non-linear pattern, and higher self-reported weekly cocaine use with worse verbal learning and memory (RAVLT total and learning rate), slower Digit Symbol and more errors and fewer correct responses on a go/no-go task, each after adjustment for age, sex and estimated IQ. At 4 weeks of enforced abstinence, three measures showed a further dose-related change beyond what their admission score predicted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that concomitant use of cocaine and alcohol may have additive negative effects on the brain compared with use of only one of the two substances (p. 2285), and the Discussion states that heavy use of alcohol alone or of cocaine alone was associated with decrements (p. 2290). Neither is tested in these data: every participant used cocaine, so there is no alcohol-alone exposure in the sample, no non-using group, and no cocaine-by-alcohol interaction term is reported at session 1, which is where additivity would have to be shown. The title's framing of differential effects of cocaine against cocaine plus alcohol likewise suggests a group comparison that the paper does not make: the two recruitment groups are never compared on test scores. The Discussion's account of maximum synergy from moderate amounts of both drugs (p. 2290) is read from a cocaine-squared term and an interaction with the admission score in the session 2 Stroop model, not from a term combining the two drugs. The suggestion that a lower threshold for alcohol effects may be related to the formation of cocaethylene (p. 2290) is offered as an idea supported by a citation, with nothing measured here. Finally, 'decrements' and 'deficits' are used throughout for scores that were never compared with a control group or with norms, and persistence at 4 weeks is inferred from non-significant change in a design the authors themselves describe as showing a practice effect in most participants.

timeline.event: Bolla, Rothman and Cadet (cited here, ref 4): dose-related neurobehavioural effects of chronic cocaine use in a smaller sample, the source of the hypothesis and of the earlier go/no-go false-positive finding this paper reports as replicated

Robinson, Heaton and O'Malley (cited here, ref 12): found the opposite direction, with people using cocaine alone performing worse than those using cocaine and alcohol; the authors attribute the discrepancy to differences in duration of use

Di Sclafani et al. compared neuropsychological performance in people dependent on crack cocaine, or on crack cocaine and alcohol, at 6 weeks and 6 months of abstinence (on the project's list; not read for this card)
Quantitative review of neurocognitive findings in people who use cocaine
Systematic critical review of long-term effects of cocaine use on cognitive functioning

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of this paper's findings, that heavier reported use goes with lower scores on some tests, is common in this literature; the contested part is what it means. One contemporary study found the opposite ordering for cocaine with and without alcohol, and the later reviews on the project's list examine whether such differences reflect drug effects, pre-existing differences or confounding. This paper adds a dose-response pattern within a single sample with enforced abstinence and a retest, and leaves cause open; the authors say a causal link would need a longitudinal study of people before and after they begin using these drugs.

funding.funder: Supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse (p. 2285).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from a university department of neurology, the intramural research programme that funded and hosted the study, and a private firm; the study was run on that programme's inpatient research unit and approved by its institutional review board and the university's (pp. 2285–2286). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort with cognitive testing before people begin using cocaine and alcohol and repeated afterwards, with exposure recorded as it happens rather than recalled and priced, and with a matched non-using comparison group retested on the same schedule so that practice effects can be separated from change; short of that, a study in this population that reports scores against norms or a demographically matched control group, and that tests a cocaine-by-alcohol interaction term directly rather than inferring additivity from separate dose-response models.

domains.note: Age, sex and estimated IQ were adjusted for, and the exposures were entered in a fixed order so cocaine effects are over and above alcohol. But education, tobacco and caffeine (permitted and never reported), route, years of use and depressive symptoms were not adjusted for; the estimated-IQ covariate is itself measured after years of use; and there is no pre-use measurement, so pre-existing differences cannot be separated from drug effects. The authors acknowledge that association, not causality, is what the design supports.

Weekly cocaine in grams was derived from recalled weekly spending at a single assumed price and purity, so the exposure inherits error from recall, from price variation and from unknown purity; where two instruments disagreed their average was taken. Urine testing confirmed recent use but not amount. Measurement error in a continuous exposure of this kind generally works against finding dose-response, but it also makes the shape of the fitted curves, on which the non-linear 'threshold' claims rest, unreliable.

Advertisement-recruited people willing to spend 30 days on a research unit without treatment, predominantly African American men who smoked cocaine, with psychiatric comorbidity and dependence on other substances excluded; all had used in the 24 to 48 hours before admission. The sample is coherent but narrow, and the exclusions remove much of the population to which the findings would be applied.

No treatment or medication was given during the 30-day stay, and the abstinence period was the same for everyone, so nothing differed systematically between people with more and less reported use after admission.

No attrition is reported, but the printed degrees of freedom range from 46 to 54 against n = 56 in ways not fully explained by the number of predictors at each step, and the number tested on each task is never given.

Standard instruments, administered in the morning by a psychometrician blind to the intensity and duration of use, which is a strength. Against that, no normative or control comparison is made, so 'decrement' is relative within the sample; and at session 2 the authors state that most participants showed the expected practice effect, which the design cannot separate from recovery because no one was retested without drug exposure.

No protocol. Tables 2 and 3 show only the tests with significant drug terms, out of a battery of at least 18 scores each tested against four or more drug terms, with no correction; results for the other tests are not given. The text also attributes the go/no-go number-correct effect to cocaine use in a way that reads as linear, while Table 2 places the significant term in the cocaine-squared column (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A carefully run inpatient study with enforced, urine-checked abstinence, blinded testing and an explicit dose-response approach, which is more than most studies in this literature offer. Its limits are structural: no comparison group of any kind, exposure derived from recalled spending, selective reporting of the tests that reached significance, and conclusions about additive effects and about alcohol alone that the data cannot address. Cite this source for dose-response associations within a sample of people who used cocaine, mostly by smoking, between self-reported weekly cocaine use and verbal learning, memory and go/no-go performance, and between self-reported weekly drinking and executive and motor test scores, at 1 to 3 days and at 4 weeks of enforced abstinence. Do not cite it for impairment relative to people who do not use these drugs, for additive or synergistic effects of cocaine and alcohol, for effects of alcohol alone, for persistence of deficits, or for anything causal.

key_findings.finding: Fifty-six people who used cocaine (29 reporting fewer than 10 drinks a week, 27 more than 10) were tested 1 to 3 days after admission and again on day 28 or 29 of a 30-day stay with enforced abstinence; all had cocaine metabolites in urine on admission, 84% (47 of 56) smoked cocaine exclusively, 80% were men and 85% African American.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants and Data collection (p. 2286); Results › Demographics and drug use (p. 2287); Discussion (p. 2291)

key_findings.finding: The two recruitment groups differed only in drinking (3.23 against 0.86 days a week and 17.51 against 3.73 drinks a week, both P < 0.05) and not in age, race, sex, education, estimated IQ, Vocabulary, depression score, years of drinking, or cocaine days, grams per week or years of use; self-reported cocaine and alcohol doses were not significantly correlated (r = -0.13).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Demographics and drug use
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the 95% interval for r = -0.13 with n = 56 runs from about -0.38 to 0.14, so independence of the two exposures is not established, only not contradicted.

key_findings.finding: At 1 to 3 days of abstinence, drinks per week predicted worse performance on Block Design, Grooved Pegboard (non-dominant hand), Trails B, Stroop Color-Word and Digit Symbol after adjustment for age, sex and estimated IQ, in every case through the squared term (for Digit Symbol through both the linear and squared terms); model R-squared totals 0.24 to 0.50.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Variables affecting performance at baseline, 2nd paragraph (p. 2288)
key_findings.note: F statistics from the text: Trails B F(1,48) = 8.23, P < 0.01; Digit Symbol linear F(1,49) = 8.05, P < 0.01 and non-linear F(1,48) = 4.75, P < 0.05; Stroop F(1,50) = 7.87, P < 0.01; Block Design F(1,50) = 4.50, P < 0.05; Grooved Pegboard F(1,46) = 6.62, P < 0.05. Editors' calculation: partial r-squared 0.08 to 0.15.

key_findings.finding: At the same session, grams of cocaine per week predicted worse verbal learning and memory and worse go/no-go performance: RAVLT total F(1,48) = 7.01, P < 0.05; RAVLT learning rate (trial 5 minus trial 1) linear F(1,48) = 4.64 and non-linear F(1,47) = 5.77, both P < 0.05; Digit Symbol F(1,47) = 6.67, P < 0.05; go/no-go false positives linear F(1,47) = 9.58, P < 0.01 and non-linear F(1,46) = 7.00, P < 0.05; go/no-go number correct F(1,47) = 14.63, P < 0.01. Verbal learning and memory were not related to alcohol dose.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 2287); Results › Variables affecting performance at baseline, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 2288)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of partial r-squared from these F statistics: 0.09 (RAVLT learning rate) to 0.24 (go/no-go number correct).

key_findings.finding: At 4 weeks of abstinence, only three measures showed a dose-related change beyond what the admission score predicted: Stroop Color-Word (cocaine squared, P < 0.01, with an admission-score by cocaine interaction, R-squared 0.67), RAVLT recognition errors (drinks per week, P < 0.01, with three interactions with the admission score, R-squared 0.53) and RAVLT delayed recall (cocaine grams per week, P < 0.05, R-squared 0.68).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Variables affecting performance after 4 weeks of abstinence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: People who performed better on admission showed less dose-related decline at retest, on the Stroop (interaction with cocaine dose F(1,48) = 5.11, P < 0.05) and on RAVLT recognition errors (interaction with alcohol F(1,48) = 5.11; linear and non-linear interactions with cocaine F(1,47) = 4.30 and F(1,46) = 5.04, all P < 0.05); the authors read this as cognitive reserve.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variables affecting performance after 4 weeks of abstinence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 4

key_findings.finding: Among the covariates, estimated IQ predicted Block Design, Digit Symbol, Trails B, Stroop and median reaction time; women scored better than men on Digit Symbol but had slower median reaction times; and older age went with slower Grooved Pegboard times in both hands.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variables affecting performance at baseline, 1st paragraph (p. 2287, continuing p. 2288)
key_findings.note: F statistics as printed, for example Stroop F(1,54) = 14.94, P < 0.01; Digit Symbol sex effect F(1,50) = 12.83, P < 0.01; non-dominant Grooved Pegboard age effect F(1,50) = 22.08.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue against reverse causation from the absence of correlation between estimated IQ and cocaine grams per week (r = 0.164) or drinks per week (r = 0.226), concluding that people with lower ability before use did not progress to heavier use.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 56): the 95% intervals run from about -0.10 to 0.41 and from -0.04 to 0.46, so a moderate positive association cannot be excluded, and the Shipley score was measured after years of use.

key_findings.finding: The authors state the study's own limits: multiple and possibly correlated dependent variables; ability to show association but not causality; limited generalizability, since 84% smoked cocaine and the sample was 80% men and 85% African American; and reliance on retrospective self-report as the main measure of drug consumption.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'There are several limitations' and the following paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows the fitted relation between drinks per week and Trails B time (higher is worse): about 66 seconds at no drinking, about 80 seconds at 3 drinks a week, and then a gradual fall to about 75 seconds at 15 drinks a week.
key_findings.note: Values read from the rendered page and approximate. The curve is a fitted line without data points or error bars; see reporting issues on how the text describes it.

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 shows RAVLT learning rate falling from about 5 words at low weekly cocaine amounts to about 0 at 9 g a week, and Figure 3 Digit Symbol correct responses falling from about 54 to about 40 over the same range.
key_findings.note: Values read from the rendered page and approximate; both are fitted lines without data points, error bars or sample sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Figure 2 defines the RAVLT learning rate as words recalled on trial 5 multiplied by words recalled on trial 1, while the figure's own axis label, the Results text and Table 2 all define it as trial 5 minus trial 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the caption at face value would mis-specify the outcome. The axis label and text agree, so the measure is the difference; anyone citing the learning-rate finding should state the subtraction.

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes the alcohol relation on Trails B as reaching a plateau above about 3 drinks a week, but Figure 1 shows performance peaking near 3 to 6 drinks and then improving steadily out to 15 drinks a week (about 80.5 down to about 75.5 seconds).
reporting_issues.page: p. 2288, with the same description repeated on p. 2290
reporting_issues.consequence: The data in the figure are an inverted-U, not a plateau. The claim that worse performance persists at higher reported drinking, used in the Discussion to argue that effects appear below the usual threshold, is not what the fitted curve shows.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the go/no-go number-correct effect as accuracy being lower with higher cocaine use, giving F(1,47) = 14.63, while Table 2 places the only significant term for that outcome in the cocaine-squared column; for RAVLT learning rate the text and table agree that both terms were significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the accuracy relation is linear or curved cannot be settled from the paper, which matters because the Discussion's argument about thresholds and about moderate amounts producing the largest effect rests on the shapes of these curves.

reporting_issues.issue: Degrees of freedom across the reported tests range from 46 to 54 against n = 56, in a way the stated model sequence does not fully explain, and the number of participants completing each test is never given, although no dropouts are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some tests appear to have missing data, which is neither quantified nor characterized; whether the people missing from particular analyses differed in reported use cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: No regression coefficients, standard errors or confidence intervals are printed, and the tables give only F statistics in the text, P thresholds as symbols and a total R-squared that includes the covariates and, at session 2, the admission score.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and direction of each dose effect can be judged only from the three fitted figures; the variance attributable to the drug terms alone cannot be recovered, so the editors computed partial r-squared from each F statistic to give a usable magnitude.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract, the title and the Discussion speak of effects of cocaine against cocaine plus alcohol, and of alcohol alone, but no analysis compares the two recruitment groups, and no cocaine-by-alcohol interaction term appears in the session 1 models; the session 2 interactions are between a dose term and the admission score.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion of additive effects does not follow from the analyses reported. The defensible statement is that the two exposures predicted different tests within one sample of people who all used cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2 and 3 list only the outcomes with significant drug terms; results for the remainder of the battery (including Trails A, the simple and choice reaction time measures, and the RAVLT recognition and delayed-recall measures at session 1) are not reported, and no correction for multiplicity was applied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion of tested associations that reached significance cannot be calculated, so the chance of false positives among the reported effects cannot be judged; the authors name this as their first limitation.

reporting_issues.issue: The cocaine exposure is a derived quantity: reported weekly spending converted at 100 US dollars per gram at 50% purity, one city-wide figure applied to everyone.
reporting_issues.consequence: The grams-per-week axis of Figures 2 and 3, and every cocaine dose effect, is proportional to reported spending. Differences in price or purity between people, places and times enter the exposure as error, and the apparent thresholds in grams should not be read as amounts of drug.
